# Local Project MCP

Install once for OpenCode. When you open a project, Local Project MCP automatically finds the nearest `mcp.json` and makes that project's local and remote servers available as native OpenCode MCP connections.

The plugin adds those server definitions to OpenCode's in-memory configuration for that project session. OpenCode runs local commands, connects to remote servers, manages OAuth, and exposes their tools. There is no MCP bridge, launch wrapper, configuration sync, background watcher, or project-specific OpenCode file to maintain.

This release targets OpenCode **1.19.4**. OpenCode's [v2 plugin API](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins) and `mcp.servers` configuration have different shapes and are not supported by this release.

## Install

Install the v0.1.1 GitHub release globally using OpenCode’s native plugin installer:

```sh
opencode plugin --global https://github.com/autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp/releases/download/v0.1.1/autobelay-opencode-project-scoped-mcp-0.1.1.tgz
```

OpenCode 1.19.4 uses `opencode plugin <module> -g` for a global install; `opencode plugin add` belongs to the separate v2 CLI. An alternative that uses the [documented global plugin directory](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/plugins/#from-local-files) is to copy the built, dependency-free `dist/plugin.js` to `~/.config/opencode/plugins/project-scoped-mcp.js`. OpenCode 1.19.4 auto-discovers `.js` and `.ts` files in that directory; it does not auto-discover `.mjs` there.

Start OpenCode in a project with a manifest:

```sh
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

Ask: “Use `project_mcp_status` to show this project's MCP connections.” The tool returns the title “Local Project MCP · Status,” which OpenCode records in its structured tool event. Native MCP tools are available separately under their generated server IDs. OpenCode 1.19.4 uses those technical IDs for native tool calls; this plugin cannot relabel their titles through its supported hooks. No project path is stored in the global installation.

## Why project-scoped tools?

An MCP server may need a particular checkout's files, branch, design tokens, or credentials. Keeping its declaration with the project lets the configuration travel with that code. A user installs this plugin once, while each project can declare its own servers without copying entries into the user's OpenCode configuration.

Local Project MCP uses OpenCode's [plugin `config` hook](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/plugins/) before native MCP connections initialize. The project manifest is read at that point. Changes to `mcp.json` take effect when the project is loaded again, such as in a new OpenCode process.

## Example: a design assistant for one application

Imagine a fictional field-notes application. Its design MCP could know the current checkout's palette, spacing, component variants, unpublished screen references, and navigation conventions. Its tools might read design tokens or explain the layout of a component. These assets and conventions belong to one application; publishing a generic public MCP would not supply them. Hosting this server remotely would require uploading or synchronizing unpublished branch-specific files. Keeping the server in the checkout lets it read the exact branch being edited. The server may still use a remote service for specific operations; local execution does not imply offline operation.

The runnable [design-studio example](examples/design-studio) is smaller. Its read-only tool returns fictional design tokens. It requires no account, credentials, cloud service, or company material:

```sh
gh repo clone autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp
cd opencode-project-scoped-mcp/examples/design-studio
opencode
```

Ask OpenCode to read the project's design tokens using its project-design MCP server.

## Project manifest

Place `mcp.json` in a checkout. The plugin walks upward from the OpenCode project directory to the nearest `mcp.json`, stopping at a Git checkout root. A nested checkout does not inherit a parent's manifest. A worktree uses the manifest and files in its own checkout. If none is found, the status tool reports that no project manifest was found.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "project-design": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "title": "Project design assistant",
      "description": "Read this checkout's design tokens and screen references.",
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["tooling/design/server.mjs"],
      "env": { "DESIGN_TOKEN_FILE": "tooling/design/tokens.json" }
    },
    "project-docs": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:DOCS_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

The remote URL is illustrative. The supported manifest transports are `stdio`, `streamable-http`, and `sse`. For local servers, `command` and `args` become OpenCode's command array, `env` becomes `environment`, and OpenCode launches the process with the manifest directory as `cwd`. For remote servers, the plugin passes the URL and headers to OpenCode, which attempts Streamable HTTP and then SSE. Generated connections use a 30-second request timeout; a native OpenCode entry can override it.

The manifest follows a practical subset of the evolving [SEP-2633 client configuration proposal](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/2633), not a finalized universal standard. OAuth fields supported here are `clientId`, `scopes` (joined into OpenCode's scope string), and `redirectUri`. Native-only OAuth options can be configured in OpenCode's override entry.

The plugin expands `${env:NAME}` references from the OpenCode process environment in manifest values. It does not read `.env` files. Do not commit credentials to a manifest. For remote servers, OpenCode can manage OAuth using the manifest's OAuth client settings, or use a configured bearer token in headers. The project must supply any runtime and credentials its servers need.

Each manifest name receives a stable OpenCode server ID of the form `project_<sanitized-name>_<twelve-character-digest>`. The digest includes the absolute manifest directory and the original name, keeping native OAuth credentials separate across projects and worktrees. OpenCode stores those credentials globally by server ID. Moving a checkout changes its generated IDs and may require signing in again, but does not require updating configuration paths. Names that sanitize alike still differ. If OpenCode already has a native MCP entry under the original manifest name, that entry wins and the plugin does not add another connection. An existing entry under the generated ID can override generated settings; `enabled: false` can disable it. `project_mcp_status` reports the manifest names, runtime IDs, and current native connection states without exposing credentials.

Manifest `title` and `description` can provide optional model guidance through OpenCode's experimental `experimental.chat.system.transform` hook. MCP discovery and connections do not depend on that guidance.

## Distribution and development

This is an independent open-source OpenCode plugin. See [distribution details](MARKETPLACE.md) and [local exercise notes](TESTING.md). It is not listed in an official OpenCode marketplace.

Global installation adds only the plugin entry to global configuration; project MCP declarations are read at runtime. The same command can be used after a machine rebuild. See [tested behavior](TESTING.md) for observed installation results.

The package exposes `dist/plugin.js` as its server entrypoint and has no runtime npm dependencies. The code is MIT licensed. [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES) accompany the bundled fictional example.

# Local Project MCP distribution

This repository distributes an independent OpenCode plugin. It is not an official OpenCode marketplace listing and is not affiliated with OpenCode or Anomaly.

Local Project MCP automatically reads the nearest project `mcp.json` and adds its local and remote servers to that project's native OpenCode MCP configuration in memory. No wrapper or configuration sync is needed.

For OpenCode 1.19.4, the plugin is a package whose `main` and `exports["./server"]` point to `dist/plugin.js`. The global `opencode plugin <module> -g` command installs a package and adds it to the user's global OpenCode configuration. Install the v0.1.1 GitHub tarball with:

```sh
opencode plugin --global https://github.com/autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp/releases/download/v0.1.1/autobelay-opencode-project-scoped-mcp-0.1.1.tgz
```

The plugin does not require npm registry publication. A repository checkout offers a direct alternative: copy `dist/plugin.js` to `~/.config/opencode/plugins/project-scoped-mcp.js`. OpenCode [loads global `.js` and `.ts` plugin files](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/plugins/#from-local-files) from that directory when it starts. Use the `.js` extension for this path; the 1.19.4 loader does not auto-discover `.mjs` files.

OpenCode's [v1 plugin documentation](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/plugins/) describes the plugin context and global plugin directory. Its [MCP documentation](https://docs.opencode.ai/docs/mcp-servers/) describes native local and remote server configuration, including `cwd` and OAuth. OpenCode v2 has a [different plugin API](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins) and [different MCP configuration](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers/); this v0.1.1 package targets v1.19.4 only.

The plugin reads a project's `mcp.json` in memory when OpenCode loads that project. It does not write MCP entries to `opencode.json`, run a separate bridge, install project servers, or access a hosted service of its own. A project manifest may start local commands or connect to remote URLs specified by that project.

The [fictional design-studio example](examples/design-studio) bundles a read-only server and a small set of sample design tokens. It demonstrates project-specific discovery without credentials or private assets. See [TESTING.md](TESTING.md) for local observations.

# Tested behavior

## v0.1.1 branding release

On 2026-10-24, `npm run build` and `npm test` completed successfully with nine synthetic tests. The packed tarball contains the bundled plugin, package metadata, README, and license. The [v0.1.1 release](https://github.com/autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp/releases/tag/v0.1.1) provides that tarball and a standalone `plugin.js` asset.

OpenCode 1.19.4 installed the release using its native `opencode plugin --global --force <tarball URL>` command. The installer added the new URL beside v0.1.0 because it treats versioned tarball URLs as different package specs. The stale v0.1.0 plugin entry was removed from global configuration; one project plugin entry remains, and the other global plugin entries were preserved.

A read-only `opencode run --format json --dir examples/design-studio` session requested only `project_mcp_status` and `read_design_tokens`. Its structured events recorded:

- `project_mcp_status` completed with `state.title` equal to `Local Project MCP · Status`, version `0.1.1`, and the example's `project-design` server connected.
- The native `read_design_tokens` call completed and returned fictional Field Notes tokens.
- No tool error states occurred.

The native MCP call retained its technical tool ID and an empty `state.title`, consistent with OpenCode 1.19.4's tool path. The custom status tool's title was verified in structured events; no rendered terminal UI claim is made here. The raw example log remains local in `/tmp` and is not published.

## v0.1.0 history

Release **v0.1.0** was installed globally from its public GitHub tarball using **OpenCode 1.19.4** on **macOS**, on 2026-10-23. Build/test tooling used **Node.js 24.22.0**. The live model runs used the existing OpenCode provider configuration.

## Installed-package observations

The native installer successfully resolved the public release, detected the server plugin entrypoint, and appended it to the existing global OpenCode plugin configuration:

```sh
opencode plugin --global https://github.com/autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp/releases/download/v0.1.0/autobelay-opencode-project-scoped-mcp-0.1.0.tgz
```

Final runs used ordinary `opencode run --format json --dir <directory>` commands. They did not use `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, project configuration generation, a local-development plugin path, or a wrapper. Prompts requested only the specified read-only tools.

| Session directory | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Existing private project | All 19 project servers connected as native MCP connections; the project-only local read-only status tool succeeded. |
| This repository's root | No manifest and zero project MCP servers. Existing unrelated global MCP configuration remained present. |
| `examples/design-studio` | One project server connected; OpenCode called its native `read_design_tokens` tool and received the fictional Field Notes tokens. |

Private-project results are summarized only. Its manifest, company identifiers, server code, credentials and raw transcripts are not published. Discovery and one read-only call do not imply every downstream tool was executed.

The earlier local-development smoke test also showed the example server in `opencode mcp list` as a normal native connection. No generic bridge connection was used.

## Automated coverage

`npm test` passed nine tests using synthetic data:

- Nearest-manifest lookup, Git checkout/worktree stopping, and missing-directory handling.
- Stdio argv, environment interpolation, manifest-relative cwd, and input immutability.
- Remote HTTP/SSE mapping, bearer-header behavior, OAuth scope/client/redirect mapping, and invalid remote options.
- Native configuration precedence, disabled generated entries, and an invalid sibling entry.
- Distinct server IDs for different projects, worktrees and names that sanitize alike.
- Credential-free status output, redacted native failures, workspace-specific status requests and optional connection guidance.
- Independent project instances and no-manifest sessions.
- Malformed-manifest reporting without echoing file contents.
- No mutation of an MCP map shared with another workspace.

The tests inspect the built plugin as well as its source helpers. They do not use private projects or external services.

## Reproduce the public example

After installation:

```sh
gh repo clone autobelay/opencode-project-scoped-mcp
cd opencode-project-scoped-mcp/examples/design-studio
opencode run 'Use only project_mcp_status and the project-design MCP read_design_tokens tool. Report the fictional tokens. Do not use shell or modify files.'
```

At the repository root, ask `project_mcp_status` for the project server count; it should be zero. `opencode mcp list` may still show unrelated servers from your existing personal configuration.

## Compatibility evidence and limits

OpenCode 1.19.4 declares and invokes an asynchronous plugin config hook before MCP initialization. Its native MCP configuration supports local `cwd`; its remote connector manages authentication and tries Streamable HTTP then SSE. Sources: [plugin hook type](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v1.19.4/packages/plugin/src/index.ts), [hook invocation](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v1.19.4/packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts), [project bootstrap](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v1.19.4/packages/opencode/src/project/bootstrap.ts), [MCP service](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v1.19.4/packages/opencode/src/mcp/index.ts).

OAuth field translation and credential-ID separation were tested synthetically. An interactive OAuth login, the manual global-plugin-file installation alternative, other operating systems, older OpenCode versions, desktop-specific sessions and the separate v2 API were not exercised. The live remote servers used their preconfigured authentication.
